summary: Río Negro legislated visibly on trans inclusion: a provincial statute reserves at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people — one of only a handful of provinces with such a law, which signals a provincial official posture better than the national baseline, though the regional surveys found none of these quota laws was actually being complied with. In a country whose trans-death counts are small enough for one provincial case to be a real signal, the 2024 national MuMaLa registry lists a named travesti victim attributed to Río Negro (with La Pampa). As everywhere, the contravención/faltas police codes remain, and the February 2025 national decrees curtailing the Gender Identity Law (minors' transition treatments; prison placement of trans detainees) apply here too.
localsOnly: The 1% travesti/trans employment statute is a resident-only mechanism a visitor never uses; its visitor-facing value is the official-posture signal it carries (non-compliant as of the surveys reviewed).

Agencia Presentes report (19 March 2026) on the Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio's 2025 tally: at least 227 hate crimes against people for sexual orientation or gender identity, up 62% year-on-year and the record of the observatory's ten years of operation — one every 38 hours; perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, beating the main modality, in a context the observatory attributes to the national government's "cultural battle" against LGBTI+ people; attacks continued in early 2026, including a life-endangering home invasion of an LGBTIQ+ organisation president in Jujuy.
